blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Blogel as an innovative graph-processing framework that introduces a two-level abstraction—vertex-centric and block-centric (collections of connected vertices)—to address inefficiencies in real-world graphs. He notes that traditional vertex-centric models struggle with large-diameter graphs (requiring excessive iterations) and high-density graphs (leading to heavy messaging), particularly in power-law networks like social or web graphs. Blogel mitigates these issues by partitioning graphs into blocks, reducing the computational workload since the number of blocks is orders of magnitude smaller than vertices. The framework supports three modes (B-mode, V-mode, VB-mode) and demonstrates significant performance gains, such as a 48x speedup on the Friendster social network due to a 372x reduction in messages. The key insight is leveraging block-level computation to optimize graph algorithms by minimizing communication overhead and iterations.
paper_title: Blogel: A Block-Centric Framework for Distributed Computation on Real-World Graphs
paper_abstract: The rapid growth in the volume of many real-world graphs (e.g., social networks, web graphs, and spatial networks) has led to the development of various vertex-centric distributed graph computing systems in recent years. However, real-world graphs from different domains have very different characteristics, which often create bottlenecks in vertex-centric parallel graph computation. We identify three such important characteristics from a wide spectrum of real-world graphs, namely (1)skewed degree distribution, (2)large diameter, and (3)(relatively) high density. Among them, only (1) has been studied by existing systems, but many real-world powerlaw graphs also exhibit the characteristics of (2) and (3). In this paper, we propose a block-centric framework, called Blogel, which naturally handles all the three adverse graph characteristics. Blogel programmers may think like a block and develop efficient algorithms for various graph problems. We propose parallel algorithms to partition an arbitrary graph into blocks efficiently, and blockcentric programs are then run over these blocks. Our experiments on large real-world graphs verified that Blogel is able to achieve orders of magnitude performance improvements over the state-ofthe-art distributed graph computing systems.
